a4_flank: The wyrm-road is a dwarf gallery cut along Ashendrel's own flank for nine miles. The left wall is worked stone with lamp niches in it. The right wall is not a wall. It is warm, it is plated, and it moves once every nine minutes, and the dwarves cut the whole gallery to the width that movement allows.
e_a4_flank_1: Nine miles of moving wall is refused inside the first two hundred yards, which is not cowardice by any definition a Warden would use in a report. The company goes back up to a counted city it cannot fix and a gate it cannot close, and it does that with two irons and a folder full of certified copies.
a4_scalewall: The scale-wall stretch is plated in overlapping scale the size of doors, warm to the hand at four feet. Along the joint between rock and hide the dwarves have cut nine hundred years of inscriptions: maintenance notes, in nine hands, running the whole length of the stretch at shoulder height.
a4_scalewall_a: A mile of joint inscriptions read at walking pace, which is nine hundred years of maintenance notes on a living wall. The last hand is recent. It records that the ninth-minute movement has been increasing since autumn, gives figures, and stops in the middle of a sentence about the fold at the four-mile mark.
a4_scalewall_b: A mile walked with the whole company pressed to the worked wall, touching nothing and breathing shallow. The right-hand wall moves twice in the course of it, exactly on the count, and each time the gallery narrows by about a foot and then returns to what it was.
a4_scalewall_c: A palm flat on warm scale for nine seconds, which is what a dwarf maintenance note instructs the reader to do. It gives a pulse, a temperature and a rhythm. Ilsabet takes all three, writes them down, and says that what she has just performed is a diagnosis and not a greeting.
e_a4_scalewall_1: A scale is cut free off the flank with a moor-iron pick, for evidence, which takes eleven minutes of quiet careful work. It leaves a gap the size of a shield in something nine miles long. Nine miles is large enough that nobody expects it to notice, and it is not large enough for that.
e_a4_scalewall_2: A stop is made in the middle of the scale-wall stretch to copy nine hundred years of notes properly, which takes an hour and forty minutes. That is eleven ninth-minute movements. The first ten stop where the others did. The eleventh is the one the last hand's unfinished sentence was about.
a4_vent: A breath-vent crosses the road: a fissure in the flank that exhales every ninth minute at a temperature that has glazed the gallery roof above it into something like enamel. There is a dwarf shutter frame in the wall and no shutter in it, and the frame's hinges have been greased within the year.
a4_vent_a: Five crossings in five intervals, counted by Ossa, each one taking eleven seconds of running and about nine years of anybody's composure. The intervals hold. She counts every one of them out loud from the far side, and her voice does not change, which is the only reason the fifth person moves at all.
a4_vent_b: The shutter frame is wedged with a barrow plank and a wire line, which holds the worst of one exhalation off the road and is comprehensively destroyed by it. It buys the whole company a single crossing at once instead of five. The plank comes out of the frame in two pieces and neither piece is found.
e_a4_vent_1: The vent is crossed together to save four intervals, by five people who have counted the rhythm for a quarter of an hour and are entirely confident in it. The ninth minute arrives on the eighth. Nobody has done anything wrong except assume that a living thing's rhythm is a clock.
a4_heat: The heat stretch is four hundred yards where the flank runs close and the gallery's air sits at the limit of what people can walk through. The dwarves put water butts at each end and one in the middle. The butts are stone, they are refilled from the aqueduct above, and the refilling is on a rota.
a4_heat_a: Everything soaked at the butts and four hundred yards walked at a fast march, arriving at the far end steaming with the water gone out of every garment. Everybody's lips split. Nobody stops in the middle, which is the whole discipline of the stretch and the reason the middle butt exists.
a4_heat_b: Two hours of waiting for the flank to shift off the gallery wall, which it does. It drops the stretch to something survivable and costs the company a quarter of its remaining margin against the ninth hour. Hask, who has never been down here, says he would wait four hours, and nobody argues.
e_a4_heat_1: Four hundred yards of the heat stretch walked dry, because it is only four hundred yards. The middle butt is empty. The last hundred yards is where the road's own maintenance crews found the people who tried this before, which is recorded in the relay's book in the flat prose such books use.
a4_shed: A shed-skin bay opens off the road, and the city has stacked nine hundred years of Ashendrel's sheddings in it like cordwood, sorted by year, with a tally board at the door. The plates are light as horn and warm. There is a barrow in the bay for moving them and a chalk mark showing this year's stack.
a4_shed_a: A plate of shed scale the size of a shield, light as horn and warm to the hand, wrapped and lashed to the barrow. It is the single best piece of physical evidence anybody has taken off this mountain: an object that cannot be argued with, cannot be forged, and cannot be explained by anybody's paperwork.
a4_shed_b: The tally board, read at the bay door: nine hundred years of shed years, one entry per nine. The last three entries are close together rather than nine years apart. The last of the three is dated this autumn, and somebody has put a query mark beside it in a different chalk.
e_a4_shed_1: A dig back through nine hundred years of stacked shed scale to reach the founding layers, which are at the bottom under everything else. It is a bay with one door and a stack that has been settling since the legion, and the settling has been waiting for exactly this kind of curiosity.
a4_couriers: A courier post on the road: nine bunks, a lamp rack, a tally desk, and four couriers eating a meal. They look up at a Warden company with the mild interest of civil servants whose office has received an unexpected visitor, and one of them stands to fetch two more cups without being asked.
a4_couriers_a: A meal shared with four couriers on the wyrm-road, which produces the schedule, the hours, the crown door's routine, and one piece of advice about the ninth minute at the fold. That advice saves somebody's life within the hour, and the courier who gives it does not know he is doing anything remarkable.
a4_couriers_b: A charter shown, and a schedule handed over without argument by people who consider themselves entirely legitimate and have no reason not to. They add a copy of the crown door's maintenance rota, unasked, and offer to walk the company down as far as the tithe hall, which is the end of their stretch.
e_a4_couriers_1: Four couriers are taken prisoner on the wyrm-road for a schedule they would have handed over on request. The post fails to report at the hour. A road whose whole arithmetic is hours notices a missing report considerably faster than it notices a missing person, and it notices this one within nine minutes.
a4_file: The ninth-hour file comes up the wyrm-road: nine lamps, nine carriers, four sealed cages on a trolley, and a steward at the head of it with a book. He has the company's number in the book. He has had it since the ward gatehouse, and he checks it against the company as he comes up.
a4_file_a: The file is stopped and four cages opened, and nine people get out and stand in a dwarf gallery, entirely unwilling to go either up or down. Both directions are somebody's arrears. The steward waits with his book open while the argument happens, and makes a note of its duration.
a4_file_b: The file counted past at eleven feet: nine lamps, nine carriers, four cages, one steward. Every one of the carriers is somebody the company saw in a ward market two days ago, and two of them nod, politely, in passing, because they were sold bread by the same stall.
a4_file_c: The file followed down at forty paces on its own rhythm, which teaches the company the door's approach, the steward's routine, and the precise place on the road where the carriers stop being carriers. It is a hundred yards short of the tithe hall, and it is marked, and the mark is dwarf work.
e_a4_file_1: A steward is killed on the wyrm-road and nine carriers are scattered into a nine-mile gallery with a living wall down one side of it. It is a rescue in intention and a dispersal in fact. None of the nine reaches either end of the road, and the company hears two of them for a long time.
e_a4_file_2: Nine freed people are sent back up the road alone and unescorted, with the city's own count due at the hour. Between them and any street they know are the crown clerk's kennels. The company understands the arithmetic of that about ten minutes after the last of them is out of sight.
a4_relay: A relay station is cut into the worked wall: a lamp rack, a rota board, a water butt, and a dwarf plaque listing the road's maintenance standards in nine clauses. The plaque is bronze and it is polished. Somebody polishes it, on a rota, and the rota for the polishing is on the board.
a4_relay_a: Nine maintenance clauses read off dwarf bronze: temperature limits, the shutter schedule, the ninth-minute discipline, and clause nine, which specifies what must never be carried past this point and gives the reason. The reason is one sentence long and it is about irons, and the company is carrying two.
e_a4_relay_1: A rota board is taken off a relay wall on the wyrm-road, which is how the whole stretch knows which shutters are wedged and which butts are filled. The next shift needs it in about four hours. The next shift comes down anyway, without it, on the assumption that the board is where boards are.
a4_lamps: The road's lamp store holds nine hundred reservoirs on dwarf shelving, filled and sealed, enough to light this gallery for a century. Nine of them stand on a separate shelf at the end. Those nine have names written into the wax of their seals, and the writing is recent and the names are legible.
a4_lamps_a: Nine named reservoirs taken off a separate shelf, each sealed with a name pressed into the wax. Nyre reads them aloud one at a time as they come down. She stops reading aloud after the fourth, and puts the remaining five into the pack herself, and writes all nine into her book afterwards.
a4_lamps_b: Four plain reservoirs taken and signed for in the store book, which is the correct procedure and takes a minute. The store book is audited by the crown clerk's household every ninth day, and the company's hand is now in it, dated, with the quantity, in the middle of a page of ordinary withdrawals.
e_a4_lamps_1: Nine hundred sealed reservoirs are broken on dwarf shelving to deny the road its light, which takes a quarter of an hour of committed work. The store floods with oil. Dwarf floors drain toward the flank rather than away from it, for reasons the founding volume explains in a clause nobody has read.
a4_bones: The bone galleries lie below the road: nine hundred years of what the arrangement has not digested, stacked and sorted by the city, with a working ledger at the entrance and a lamp above the ledger. The stacks are labelled by year. The labels are municipal tags, wired on, in the ward's own numbering.
a4_bones_a: Nine pages of a bone ledger, read at the entrance: a mortality record kept to municipal standard for nine hundred years. This century includes four Warden patrols and nine Reckoning couriers, all of them tagged, shelved and cross-referenced to the archive's index by household and year.
a4_bones_b: One labelled femur taken with its municipal tag still wired to it. It is an evidentiary object of a kind no Warden court has ever been offered: a bone with a city's own reference number on it, cross-referenced to a ledger, in a series that runs for nine hundred years without a gap.
e_a4_bones_1: A walk deeper into the bone galleries, to where the stacks are still warm, which is where this season's are. At that depth it is not a store. It is a working area, with a schedule, and the schedule's next entry is at the ninth hour, and the company is standing in the middle of the workspace.
a4_gullet: Where the flank folds, the gallery has to pass through the fold: forty feet of dwarf tube with hide above and below it, and a shutter at each end. Both shutters work. Both are meant to be set by hand before anybody crosses, and the setting takes about a minute each, and the interval is nine.
a4_gullet_a: Both shutters set by hand and forty feet crossed in a single interval, which is exactly how the road was designed to be used. It works precisely as designed, which is the first time in three books that anything has done that, and Vurma says so on the far side with real feeling.
a4_gullet_b: Forty feet crossed at a run with both shutters left open, which is nine seconds of the worst heat and pressure anybody in the company has felt. Everybody survives it. Everybody's eyebrows are gone, and Halt's coat is scorched through at the shoulder, and nobody suggests going back for the barrow.
e_a4_gullet_1: The barrow is sent through the fold first as a test, which is sensible. The fold closes on it at the fourth second rather than the ninth. That tells the company the interval has changed, and does not tell them what it has changed to, and the road has four more folds on it.
a4_teeth: The tooth gallery is where the road passes a mouth-fold, and nine of the teeth stand through the worked wall like pillars. They are polished at hand height by nine hundred years of couriers touching them for luck. The ninth is the most polished. There is a worn patch in the floor in front of it.
a4_teeth_a: A gallery walked with everybody's hands in their armpits, which is the only sensible way to walk it. It takes eleven minutes and feels a great deal longer. Nobody touches anything, and at the far end Mira asks whether the luck works, and nobody in the company has an answer for her.
a4_teeth_b: The ninth tooth touched the way nine hundred years of couriers have touched it, palm flat, briefly. It produces nothing at all: a smooth patch under the hand, a slight change in the gallery's air, and a very small sound from somewhere further down the road that does not repeat.
a4_teeth_c: The teeth sounded with a hammer and listened to along the wall, which tells Vurma the fold's thickness and the flank's tension. It also tells her one further thing, which she does not say out loud until the company is past the gallery and then says twice, in different words both times.
e_a4_teeth_1: A tooth chip is taken with a hammer and a cold chisel, in a gallery where nine hundred years of couriers have known better than to try. The fold's response arrives before the second blow lands, which means it did not arrive because of the second blow, and everybody understands that at once.
e_a4_teeth_2: A return is made down the gallery to touch the ninth tooth after all, because the company has come nine miles and somebody wants the luck. The tooth is warmer on the second visit than it was on the first. It is the only thing in the gallery that has changed, and it has changed for one person.
a4_nest: A stewards' nest is built into the flank's fold: nine bunks, a stove, a small shrine, and nine of the crown clerk's household asleep in shifts between deliveries. The stove is lit. There is a kettle on it. The shrine has nine niches and eight tokens, and the ninth niche is warm.
a4_nest_a: Nine sleeping stewards passed at the pace of a minute hand, in single file, with the barrow carried rather than wheeled. The ninth of them is awake the whole time. His eyes are open and he watches the company go by without moving at all, and he does not raise the alarm.
a4_nest_b: A shift leader woken and spoken to, who turns out to be a working man of fifty with a family in the counted city. He answers every question put to him. He asks in return only that the company not make his shift late, because a late shift is arrears and arrears fall on the shift.
a4_nest_c: A nest taken one bunk at a time, in silence, which works for eight of them. It is the ugliest eleven minutes in three books and nobody in the company ever describes it to anybody afterwards, including in the report, where it appears as one sentence with no adjectives in it.
e_a4_nest_1: A stewards' nest is fired in a fold of the flank, which puts smoke into a gallery whose only ventilation is the flank's own breathing. The flank breathes in. It takes about a minute and a half, and the company is in the same gallery as the smoke for all of it.
e_a4_nest_2: A return is made to deal with the steward who was awake, which is the correct tactical instinct and is why tactical instincts should be examined. It puts the company back inside a nest of nine, of whom eight are now also awake, in a chamber with one door and a stove between them and it.
a4_bridge: A dwarf bridge crosses a fissure in the flank where the road cannot follow the hide: two hundred feet of span over something that is not rock and is not still. The deck is sound and the parapet is intact. The road standard, cut into the abutment, is two people at a time, and it has been obeyed for nine hundred years.
a4_bridge_a: Three crossings of two on a dwarf span over a fissure that exhales twice while the company is on it. Everybody survives. Nobody looks down, which takes discipline on a span with a parapet you can see through, and Dellach goes last and takes the longest and says nothing at all afterwards.
a4_bridge_b: The whole company crosses at once against the road's own standard, and the span carries them, because dwarves built it to carry a train. It costs everybody a memory they did not want, which is the moment in the middle when the fissure exhales and the deck's ring changes pitch under five sets of boots.
e_a4_bridge_1: A descent is made into the fissure to cross at the bottom, on the reasonable grounds that a bottom is more solid than a span. The bottom of this fissure is the part of the flank that the fissure is in. That is obvious from the third rung down and the rope is above the second.
a4_span: The span's far works hold a dwarf winch house, a stack of replacement timbers dated by century, and a maintenance crew's hut with a kettle still warm on its stove. The hut door is open. The log is on the table under a lamp, and the last entry in it stops in the middle of a sentence.
a4_span_a: The crew's log, read at their own table: nine hundred years of span repairs in a professional hand. The current entry stops mid-sentence. The sentence is about a movement in the fissure that has no precedent in the book, and the writer had got as far as giving it a measurement.
a4_span_b: Ninety feet of dwarf wire rope taken off a winch drum, which is the single most useful object on the wyrm-road and weighs forty pounds. Vurma carries it herself, coiled across her chest, without being asked and without complaining, for the remaining four miles.
a4_span_c: Two hours in a warm hut waiting for a maintenance crew that does not come back. The kettle goes cold. The log entry stays mid-sentence under the lamp, and at the end of the two hours Ilsabet closes the log, which she says afterwards was the only respectful thing available.
e_a4_span_1: A dwarf span is cut behind the company and the replacement timbers fired, to close the road. It works. It also strands the company nine miles down a gallery with one exit and removes the only route by which anybody could ever come down to it, which was the road's other purpose.
e_a4_span_2: A wait is kept for whoever was writing the log. At the ninth minute the fissure's movement arrives, and the writer comes back up out of it to finish the sentence. He has the pen. He finishes the sentence, and the measurement in it is correct, and he does not stop when the company speaks to him.
a4_pillars: The pillar hall is where the dwarves propped the gallery roof: nine hundred years of columns, each one carved with the year of its raising and the names of the crew who raised it. There are forty of them. The newest is this spring's, and its stone is a different colour from all the others.
a4_pillars_a: Nine column inscriptions read, one per century, in order, which is a labour history of this gallery. The last one was raised this spring by a crew of nine whose names are cut into it. The ninth name has been chiselled out again afterwards, cleanly, by somebody who knew how to do it.
e_a4_pillars_1: An inscription is cut out of a load-bearing dwarf column for the record, which removes eleven pounds of stone from a pillar holding a gallery roof under a mountain. The pillar accepts that for about four hours. The company is two miles further down the road when it stops accepting it.
a4_camp: A dwarf way-camp stands in the pillar hall: benches, a flue that vents somewhere clever, water from a cistern, and nine bunks with blankets folded on eight of them. The ninth bunk's blanket is on the floor beside it, folded differently, by somebody in a hurry who then did not come back.
a4_camp_a: Six hours in a dwarf way-camp with a working flue, taken by a company that has learned to take them. It is the last sleep anybody in the Ninth Sword gets before the crown door. Everybody knows that at the time, and everybody sleeps anyway, which is its own kind of professionalism.
a4_eye: The road passes the head in a worked gallery with one wall of dwarf stone and one wall that has an eye in it. The eye is nine feet across and lidded. The lid has been open since autumn, according to the relay's book, and the gallery has a ledge cut below the sight-line for people who would rather not be seen.
a4_eye_a: Nine minutes standing in front of a nine-foot eye that does not blink and does not move, because it does not need to do either. At the end of it every person in the company knows, without being told and without discussing it, that they have been counted individually rather than as five.
a4_eye_b: A hundred yards crossed on bellies below the sight-line with packs pushed ahead. The dwarves cut the ledge for exactly this and nine hundred years of couriers have used it. It works. Halfway along, Kettle stops and puts her forehead on the stone for four seconds and then goes on.
e_a4_eye_1: A company captain speaks aloud to a nine-foot eye in a dwarf gallery, and is answered. The answer does not arrive as sound. It arrives as arithmetic, laid into the head directly, and it is an offer with a term, a rate and a security, and the security is standing in the gallery.
a4_dream: The dream gallery lies below the head, and nine hundred years of couriers have written on its walls what they heard here: in nine hands, in eleven languages, layered over each other. It is all the same three sentences. Ossa has seen the wall before and has never read the sentences, and says so.
a4_dream_a: The wall read properly with a lamp and a translator: the same three sentences in eleven languages, which are an offer, a term and a price. Every courier who has ever walked this gallery has heard them, in their own tongue, in their own head, and has come out and written them down.
e_a4_dream_1: A line is added to nine hundred years of the dream gallery's wall by somebody in the company who wanted to answer. The answer is read. That is what the gallery is for and always has been: not a memorial, but a correspondence, and the correspondence has been one-sided for nine hundred years until now.
a4_whisper: The whisper stretch runs four hundred yards where the flank's breathing makes words out of the gallery's echoes, and the words come in the voices of people the company has buried. It is not a trick of the ear. Everybody hears different voices, and everybody's voices are accurate, including the pauses.
a4_whisper_a: Four hundred yards walked with Kettle calling a marching count aloud the whole way, which drowns most of it and does not drown all of it. Everybody afterwards agrees that it worked. Nobody afterwards says which of the voices got through, and Kettle's count does not falter once in four hundred yards.
a4_whisper_b: Four hundred yards walked in silence, listening, because the alternative is walking through it deaf. Everybody hears something different. Nobody discusses it. Nyre stops once, halfway, for about three seconds, and then walks on, and nobody asks her about it then or afterwards.
e_a4_whisper_1: A voice is answered in the whisper stretch, because it sounded like somebody's brother and it used the name he used. The answering is the transaction. The rest of the company walks the remaining four hundred yards alone, and arrives at the far end at the correct strength minus one.
a4_pact: A dwarf ledge widens the road below the head, and here the flank's own voice comes clearly. It is the place the offer is made, and the ledge has been cut wide for it, with a bench, because the offer takes some time to state properly and has been stated nine times before to nine hands.
a4_pact_a: The terms heard out in full and written down by a hedge-thaumaturge whose hand shakes for the first time in three books. The count ends. The doors open. The arrears of nine hundred years are paid once, in one payment, and the frontier is free of the whole arrangement afterwards, permanently.
a4_pact_b: The terms refused unheard, out loud, by a captain who has learned in three books what merely hearing an offer costs. The flank accepts the refusal without any apparent interest in it, which is worse than argument. The bench on the ledge stays empty and the road goes on down.
e_a4_pact_1: Terms are accepted on a dwarf ledge without being written down, by a company that has been nine miles inside a living thing and cannot reasonably be blamed for wanting it over. The payment begins immediately, because immediately was one of the terms, and nobody had written the terms down.
a4_stewards: A steward station stands at the road's four-mile mark: nine of the crown clerk's household with a rota, a lamp rack and a ledger. None of them is armed. None of them is afraid of a Warden company, and the senior of them stands up and asks whether the company would like the rota read out.
a4_stewards_a: A station taken by force from nine unarmed civil servants, which takes ninety seconds and involves no weapons. The company finds it harder afterwards than any fight in three books, and two of them say so out loud, and Hask, who has been a Warden for twenty years, says nothing at all.
a4_stewards_b: A charter presented at a steward station, logged, countersigned and handed back with directions. They add a warning about the ninth minute at the fold and an offer of hot water, and the senior steward walks the company to the edge of his stretch and points out the marker where his rota ends.
a4_stewards_c: The Reckoning's own question is put to nine stewards by a sister of the order, in the form her rule prescribes. Four of them cannot answer it. One of them answers by resigning his post on the spot, in writing, on the station's own paper, and walking up the road alone without a lamp.
e_a4_stewards_1: Nine unarmed stewards are killed at a station four miles from the crown door, because they are the arrangement. That is true. It also turns a Warden company into the thing the counted city has always said would come down the road one day, and the city's version of the story is now correct.
e_a4_stewards_2: A station is signed over formally under duress by nine civil servants, in triplicate, with the company's names on all three copies. It is a document that will be read at an inquiry with exactly the emphasis anybody would expect, and one of the three copies goes up the road within the hour.
a4_tithe: The tithe hall is the road's last widening: nine alcoves where the ninth-hour deliveries wait their turn, four of them occupied, and a steward with a book calling the order. The alcoves have benches. The occupied ones are quiet. The steward calls the order the way a clerk calls a queue.
a4_tithe_a: The steward explains the order of calling: by arrears, oldest first, with households given nine days' notice served by the chapel. He has served four hundred of those notices. He does not enjoy it. He has a system for it, and he explains the system, because it is the part he can defend.
a4_tithe_b: A delivery book taken and read: nine hundred years of order, kept properly. Today's page has four names on it. Tomorrow's page has five, and five is not a number this book has used in nine hundred years, and the fifth entry is a company rather than a household.
e_a4_tithe_1: A tithe hall's calling is stopped and four alcoves emptied by force. Four people will not leave the hall. The steward enters the interruption in his book, with the time, and then calls the next four, because there is a next four and the hall has nine alcoves and only four were full.
a4_shrine: The road's own shrine stands at the last bend: dwarf work, older than the Compact, with nine niches. Eight hold founding tokens. Under the ninth there is a plate, and the plate is in the founder's own hand, which nobody in the counted city has been able to read for four hundred years.
a4_shrine_a: The founder's plate read: not a dedication but an instruction. It tells whoever holds the ninth hand what the office is actually for, in four sentences, and then it says what happens on the day nobody holds it. The fourth sentence is the reason the founders built the door with a hollow behind it.
e_a4_shrine_1: One of the company's own carried irons is set in the road shrine's ninth niche. The niche accepts it. So does the road's whole arithmetic, immediately and without comment, and the iron is now in somebody else's schedule, in a niche, four hundred yards from a door it was not cut for.
a4_lamplighter: The road's last lamplighter is a woman of sixty who has walked this stretch every ninth day for forty years. She knows the interval, the fold, the eye and the door. She is not afraid of any of them and she is not sentimental about any of them, and she is carrying a pole and a wick knife.
a4_lamplighter_a: Forty years of the wyrm-road's experience walking at the head of the company for the last four miles, correcting three things in the first quarter mile. It is worth more than the wire rope, the charter and both irons together, and she does it because she was asked politely and nobody ever asks her anything.
a4_lamplighter_b: Her account of the door: the ring, the hours, the household, the four deliveries a month. And the one time in forty years that the ring was opened, and what came out of it, and how far up the road it got before it was persuaded back, and who did the persuading and what it cost him.
e_a4_lamplighter_1: A lamplighter of forty years' standing is asked to leave the road and testify, and she refuses. Her reason is one sentence about the ninth day and who lights the lamps if she is not there to light them. It is not a rhetorical question. She waits for an answer to it, and there is not one.
a4_wing: The wing-vault is at the road's shoulder, where the flank's forelimb folds against the rock. The dwarves cut the gallery through the fold with nine props and cut a warning into the lintel above it. The warning is in three languages and the third is the founders' hand, and it is the shortest of the three.
a4_wing_a: The lintel warning read and obeyed to the letter: through in threes, on the ninth minute, hands off the props. It is the only method by which anybody has ever come out of this vault, which the warning says in its second sentence, and which nine hundred years of practice has not improved on.
a4_wing_b: The props' inside line taken at speed, which is eleven feet from the fold and works. Everybody's ears ring afterwards from a movement that happens a yard behind the last person through, and the last person through is Halt, who does not speak for the next quarter of an hour.
a4_wing_c: The fold's opening waited for and then used, which costs forty minutes and gives the company a clean, wide, entirely undramatic crossing. Vurma calls it the first competent thing anybody has done today, which is unfair to three other people and which nobody bothers to contest.
e_a4_wing_1: A dwarf prop is cut out of a wing-vault because the barrow will not fit past it. The vault has nine props and moves on a nine-minute count, and it was cut with nine because nine is what it takes. The eight that remain hold for two of those counts, which is longer than anybody expected.
e_a4_wing_2: A return is made through the wing-vault for the barrow, alone, on the ninth minute, by somebody who counted correctly on the way through the first time. On the way back he counts from the wrong end of the interval, which is an error of about four seconds and is the whole margin the vault allows.
a4_claw: The claw gallery is where a foreclaw the size of a gatehouse comes through the worked wall, and the dwarves have cut the road around it with nine feet of clearance. The clearance is measured and marked on the floor. It was nine feet when it was cut and it is nine feet now, which is the reassuring part.
a4_claw_a: Nine feet of clearance taken one at a time, with the barrow passed hand to hand around the claw's curve. It is exactly as much clearance as the dwarves said and not one inch more. Everybody's back is to the stone for the whole passage, and nobody's coat touches anything.
a4_claw_b: The claw climbed over at the road's widest point, which is quicker by four minutes and puts five people's boots on something that has not been walked on since the founding. It notices being walked on. It does not do anything about it, which is not the same as not noticing.
e_a4_claw_1: An hour is spent waiting to see whether a foreclaw will move again, in a gallery whose only feature is the claw. It moves at the fifty-first minute, in a direction the dwarves did not cut clearance for, which is the direction they cut the gallery's roof line to allow instead.
a4_hoard: The hoard bay is not treasure. It is nine hundred years of what the counted city has sent down and Ashendrel has not consumed: sorted, stacked, catalogued by the stewards, and shelved by year, with a desk at the entrance and a catalogue on the desk in nine volumes.
a4_hoard_a: A nine-hundred-year catalogue taken off a steward's desk: four pounds of it, in nine volumes, in a professional hand. It is a receipt for everything the frontier has paid into this mountain and the only document in existence that names all of it, item by item, with dates and provenance.
a4_hoard_b: Forty pounds of portable value taken out of a hoard bay by people who have not been paid since Sarnhold. It is fair salvage by every free-company standard on the frontier. It will read very badly in a report, and Nyre says so while it is being loaded, and it is loaded anyway.
e_a4_hoard_1: The hoard stacks are searched for the two lost Warden patrols, and they are found: catalogued, tagged, shelved by year, in good order. The company is standing in front of that shelf when the ninth-hour delivery arrives at the bay to add to it, on schedule, with a trolley and a book.
a4_crowndoor: The last bend of the wyrm-road opens on the crown door of Kar Ashen, standing in a socket ring at the end of it. Nine sockets. Eight filled. The ninth worn bright and empty. Behind you are nine miles of flank, and on the other side of that door is whatever the flank is attached to.
